title: Ethiopian Mustard Greens
community: Ethiopian highlands — the indigenous Ethiopian green
author: Mama Tigist
desc: Ethiopian Ye'abesha Gomen — the traditional Ethiopian mustard greens (Ethiopian kale, Brassica carinata), more peppery and bitter than collard greens, cooked with onion, garlic, and green jalapeños. The indigenous Ethiopian green — more intensely flavoured than ordinary collard greens.
longDesc: Ye'abesha Gomen ('Ethiopian greens') refers specifically to the Ethiopian kale (Brassica carinata) — an indigenous Ethiopian plant with a more complex, slightly peppery flavour than the collard greens used in standard Gomen. When available, it is preferred by Ethiopian cooks for its more authentic and complex flavour.
ingredients: 500g Ethiopian kale or mustard greens (or collard greens)
steps: Blanch in boiling water 3 minutes. Drain.
Heat oil. Cook onion until golden.
Add garlic and jalapeño. Cook 2 minutes.
Cook 10 minutes, stirring, until wilted and fragrant.
chefTips: Ethiopian kale (Brassica carinata) is more bitter than collard greens — blanching is more important.
The green jalapeño (not berbere) provides the heat for greens — this is correct.
commonMistakes: Not blanching — the peppery bitterness is too intense raw.
cookingScience: Ethiopian kale (Brassica carinata) contains higher concentrations of glucosinolates than collard greens — these compounds are both more pungent and more nutritionally valuable. The blanching step converts some of these glucosinolates to isothiocyanates (anti-cancer compounds) via myrosinase enzyme activity.
sustainabilityTips: Brassica carinata is an indigenous Ethiopian plant — growing it supports biodiversity and traditional agriculture.
servedWith: With Doro Wat and Kitfo — the most traditional pairing
healthBenefits: Highest glucosinolate content of the Ethiopian greens.
More nutritionally dense than collard greens.
culturalNote: Ye'abesha Gomen is the authentic Ethiopian green — the kale that has been grown in Ethiopian highlands for thousands of years, the green that appears in the oldest Ethiopian cooking traditions. Finding it outside Ethiopia requires Ethiopian specialty markets; when found, its superior flavour is immediately evident.
